decks.title: Era of One-Party Dominance — Part 1: The First Three Elections
goals: Explain why India's first general election was a test for democracy and how it was organised
Describe the role of the Election Commission and the use of symbols
Compare the results of the 1952, 1957 and 1962 elections
Explain how first-past-the-post gave the Congress more seats than votes

slides.heading: Era of One-Party Dominance
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **first three general elections** and how one party came to dominate.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why the first election was a test, the Election Commission, voting with symbols, the three elections, seats and votes, and Kerala in 1957
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Imagine organising an election in which about seventeen crore people vote, most of them for the first time, and most of them cannot read. That was India in 1951. In this part we see how the country met that challenge, what the first three elections produced, and why one party won so many seats.

slides.heading: Why 1951 was a test
slides.body_md: India gave **every adult** the vote at once, in a poor and largely non-literate society.

rows: About 17 crore adults, most voting for the first time
Electoral rolls prepared and constituencies drawn
A vast country with poor roads
Peaceful polls; results accepted by losers

visual.alt: Table of the challenges of the first election and responses: a huge new electorate met by rolls and constituencies; non-literate voters met by symbols; a vast country met by polling over months; doubts met by peaceful polls whose results losers accepted
visual.caption: Figures are approximate.

slides.narration: Many observers doubted that a poor country, where most people could not read, could hold a free election with every adult voting. The table shows each challenge and how it was met: new electoral rolls, symbols for candidates, polling spread over months, and finally a peaceful result that the losers accepted.

slides.heading: The Election Commission
slides.body_md: Set up in **January 1950**. The first **Chief Election Commissioner** was **Sukumar Sen**.
bullets: Prepared electoral rolls and drew constituencies
Trained lakhs of polling staff
Polling ran from late 1951 into early 1952
slides.narration: The Election Commission was created in January 1950, just as the Constitution came into force. Its first head, Sukumar Sen, had to prepare voter lists, draw constituency boundaries and train lakhs of staff. Because the task was so large, voting was spread over several months, which is why we call it the election of 1951 to 1952.

visual.caption: The era of one-party dominance at a glance

slides.narration: This timeline covers the whole chapter. The Election Commission comes first, in 1950. The Jana Sangh is founded in 1951 and the first Lok Sabha meets in 1952. In 1957 Kerala elects a communist government. In 1959 the Swatantra Party is founded and the Kerala government is dismissed. The third election follows in 1962, and the communists split in 1964.

slides.heading: Quick check: why the doubts?
slides.body_md: Why did many observers doubt that India could hold a free election in 1951?
slides.narration: Think about who was being given the vote, and what the country was like at the time.

slides.heading: Voting when most could not read
slides.body_md: Each candidate had a **symbol**; voters put the ballot in the box with that symbol.

rows: A separate box for each candidate, marked with a symbol
One ballot paper with all names and symbols, marked with a stamp
Electronic voting machines; used across the country by 2004

visual.alt: Table of voting methods: separate boxes with symbols in the first two elections; one ballot paper with names and symbols later; electronic voting machines from the late 1990s, used across the country by 2004

slides.narration: How do you vote if you cannot read names? In the first two elections, each candidate had a separate box marked with a symbol, such as a lamp or a pair of bullocks. Later a single ballot paper carried all names and symbols. From the late 1990s electronic voting machines came in, and by 2004 they were used all over the country.

slides.heading: Quick check: symbols
slides.body_md: Which arrangement helped non-literate voters in the early elections?
slides.narration: Look for the option that keeps the vote both correct and secret.

slides.heading: A peaceful verdict
slides.body_md: The polls were **peaceful**, turnout was reasonable, and **losers accepted** the result.
bullets: Democracy was shown to work in a poor country
The Congress won a large majority
Jawaharlal Nehru continued as Prime Minister
slides.narration: The election passed off peacefully and its results were accepted, including by those who lost. That acceptance matters as much as the voting itself. The Congress won a big majority and Jawaharlal Nehru continued as Prime Minister. The world saw that adult franchise could work even where poverty and illiteracy were widespread.

slides.heading: Three elections, one pattern

rows: About three-quarters of Lok Sabha seats

visual.alt: Table of the first three elections: in 1951 to 1952, 1957 and 1962 the Congress won roughly three-quarters of Lok Sabha seats with under half of the votes; Kerala elected a communist government in 1957; the opposition remained divided
visual.caption: Shares are rounded and approximate.

slides.narration: Look at the three elections side by side. Each time the Congress won roughly three-quarters of the seats in the Lok Sabha. Yet its share of votes stayed below half. Kerala in 1957 was the notable exception at the state level. Why should seats and votes differ so much? The next slides answer that question.

slides.heading: First-past-the-post
slides.body_md: In each constituency the candidate with the **most votes** wins, even without a majority.

nodes.label: Most votes wins (not necessarily a majority)
Largest party can win far more seats than its vote share

visual.alt: Flow: many candidates contest a constituency; the one with the most votes wins even without a majority; this repeats in every constituency; so the largest party can win far more seats than its share of votes
visual.caption: First-past-the-post

slides.narration: India elects the Lok Sabha by the first-past-the-post system. Whoever gets the most votes in a constituency wins, even with forty per cent. If one party is strong everywhere and its rivals split the remaining votes, that party can win seat after seat. Across the country, its share of seats then rises far above its share of votes.

Step 2 — Count seats: P 4, Q 1, R 0.
Step 3 — Vote share of P: 186 ÷ 500 × 100 = 37.2%.
Step 4 — Seat share of P: 4 ÷ 5 × 100 = 80%; gap 42.8 percentage points.

Now add the votes: P has 186 thousand out of 500 thousand, about thirty-seven per cent. So P has eighty per cent of the seats with well under half of the votes, because Q and R split the rest.

slides.heading: Kerala, 1957
slides.body_md: The **CPI** won Kerala in 1957 — a communist party in power **through the ballot**.

rows: CPI wins the Kerala assembly election; E. M. S. Namboodiripad becomes Chief Minister
Land and education reforms proposed; strong protests by opponents
Centre dismisses the government under Article 356 (President's Rule)

visual.alt: Table on Kerala: in 1957 the CPI won and E. M. S. Namboodiripad became Chief Minister; reforms and protests followed; in 1959 the Centre dismissed the government under Article 356

slides.narration: Kerala gave the first big surprise. In 1957 the Communist Party of India won the state election, and E. M. S. Namboodiripad became Chief Minister. It was rare anywhere in the world for communists to take office through a free vote. After two years of protests, the Centre dismissed the government in 1959 under Article 356, which began a long debate.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a five-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: describe the first general election and why it mattered.
bullets: Step 1 — Note five headings before writing.
Step 2 — One fact per heading.
Step 3 — End with the significance.

rows: Who ran it: Election Commission (1950), Sukumar Sen
Scale: about 17 crore adults, new rolls
Method: symbols, separate boxes, months of polling
Meaning: adult franchise can work in a poor, non-literate society

visual.alt: Planning table for a five-mark answer on the first election: who ran it, scale, method, outcome and meaning

slides.narration: Five-mark answers reward five clear points. Before you write, jot down five headings: who ran the election, how big it was, how people voted, what happened, and why it mattered. Put one solid fact under each heading. Ending with the significance turns a list of facts into an answer that earns full marks.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Set up 1950; first CEC Sukumar Sen
1952, 1957, 1962: about three-quarters of seats for Congress

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the Election Commission and Sukumar Sen, the first election and symbols, three elections, seats versus votes, and Kerala

slides.narration: To sum up. The Election Commission, led first by Sukumar Sen, organised a huge election in 1951 to 1952 using symbols and separate boxes. In 1952, 1957 and 1962 the Congress won about three-quarters of the seats with less than half the votes, thanks to first-past-the-post and a divided opposition. Kerala in 1957 was the exception.

slides.heading: Exam tips

rows: One party was dominant in free, competitive elections
It won most seats with less than half of the votes

visual.alt: Exam tips table: India was dominant-party, not one-party; the Congress won most seats with under half the votes; Swatantra was founded only in 1959

slides.narration: Watch out for three common slips. Never call India a one-party state; it had one dominant party in free elections. Do not say the Congress won a majority of votes; it won a majority of seats. And remember the Swatantra Party came only in 1959, so it did not contest the first two elections.

decks.title: Era of One-Party Dominance — Part 2: The Congress System and the Opposition
goals: Distinguish a dominant-party democracy from a one-party system
Explain the Congress as a social and ideological coalition that tolerated factions
Explain the role of the opposition in the 1950s
Describe the ideas and origins of the Socialist Party, the CPI, the Jana Sangh and the Swatantra Party

slides.heading: The Congress System and the Opposition
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **why** the Congress dominated, and **who** opposed it.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: what dominance means, the Congress as a coalition, factions, why the opposition mattered, and four early opposition parties
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 1 we saw that one party won election after election. Now we ask why, and what kind of party it was. We will also meet the small opposition parties of the time and see why they mattered far more than their seat numbers suggest.

slides.heading: Dominance is not one-party rule
slides.body_md: Other parties were **legal**, contested freely and **criticised** the government.

visual.alt: Comparison table: in a dominant-party democracy other parties are legal and elections free; in a one-party system other parties are banned; India from 1952 to 1967 was the first kind

slides.narration: Some countries have only one legal party. India was different. Here many parties contested freely, and the Congress won because voters chose it. So we call this dominance within a democracy, not a one-party system. This difference is the starting point for every answer in this chapter.

sections.heading: 1. The first general election (1951–52)
sections.body_md:
**Election Commission:** created in **January 1950**; first Chief Election Commissioner **Sukumar Sen**.

**The challenge:** universal adult franchise for about **17 crore** adults in a poor, mostly non-literate society. Tasks included preparing electoral rolls, drawing constituencies and training lakhs of polling staff. Polling ran from **October 1951** into **early 1952**.

**Method:** a **symbol** for each candidate and a separate box per candidate (first two elections); later a single ballot paper with all names and symbols; electronic voting machines from the late 1990s, used across the country by 2004.

**Result:** peaceful polls; the losers accepted the outcome; the Congress won a big majority and Jawaharlal Nehru remained Prime Minister. The election showed that adult franchise could work in a poor country.

sections.heading: 2. The second and third elections and Kerala
sections.body_md:
**1957 and 1962:** the Congress again won roughly **three-quarters** of Lok Sabha seats.

**Kerala, 1957:** the **Communist Party of India** won the assembly election; **E. M. S. Namboodiripad** became Chief Minister. A communist party coming to power through a free vote was rare in the world. After protests against its reforms, the Centre **dismissed** the government in **1959** under **Article 356**, which started a lasting debate on the use of President's Rule.

In the **first-past-the-post** system the candidate with the **most votes** in a constituency wins, even without 50 per cent.

The Congress was present in every constituency, while the opposition was **divided** among several parties. So it won most seats with **less than half** of the votes.

sections.heading: 4. The nature of Congress dominance
sections.body_md:
**Dominant party, not one party:** opposition parties were legal and elections free.

**Why the Congress dominated:**
- **Legacy** of the national movement and well-known leaders.
- **Organisation** spread across the country before the first election.
- **Social coalition:** support from many classes, castes, religions and regions.
- **Ideological coalition:** left, right and centre inside one party; policies usually in the middle.
- **Tolerance of factions:** groups competed inside the party, acting as an internal check and reducing exits.
- A **divided opposition**.

key_terms.definition_md: A group within a party, based on ideas or loyalty to a leader.
A combination of groups; for the Congress, of social groups and ideas within one party.

sections.heading: 5. The opposition parties
sections.body_md:
**Socialist Party:** from the Congress Socialist Party (1934); separate from **1948** when the Congress stopped allowing organised groups with their own constitutions; democratic socialism; later split into several parties.

**Communist Party of India:** communist groups active from the 1920s; Marxism-Leninism; largest opposition group in the first Lok Sabha; won Kerala in 1957; split in **1964** (the CPI(M) was formed).

**Bharatiya Jana Sangh:** founded **1951**; founder-president **Syama Prasad Mukherjee**; stressed national and cultural unity and Hindi as the official language; limited seats, support mainly in parts of the north.

**Swatantra Party:** founded **1959** after the Congress Nagpur resolution (land ceilings, state trading in food grains, cooperative farming); leaders included **C. Rajagopalachari**; wanted less state control and free enterprise.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1950. The Election Commission was set up in January 1950, just as the Constitution came into force. 1947 is the year of independence, 1952 the year the first election ended and the first Lok Sabha met, and 1957 the year of the second general election.

Votes were cast in 1951 but counted only after a year
Only the states voted in 1951 and the Lok Sabha in 1952

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Polling was spread over several months, from late 1951 into early 1952. Because of the size of the country and the electorate, polling was held in phases from October 1951 to early 1952; the first Lok Sabha met in 1952. There was no cancelled round, no year-long counting delay, and Lok Sabha and many assembly polls were held together.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined village of 1951, most voters cannot read. Which arrangement used in the early elections helped them vote for the candidate they wanted?

options.text_md: Voters wrote the name of their candidate on a blank slip
Voters told the polling officer their choice aloud
Each candidate had a symbol, and voters placed the ballot in the box marked with that symbol
Only literate members of each family were allowed to vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Each candidate had a symbol, and voters placed the ballot in the box marked with that symbol. Symbols on separate ballot boxes allowed people who could not read to vote secretly and correctly. Writing names would exclude non-literate voters, saying one's choice aloud breaks the secret ballot, and the Constitution gave every adult the vote regardless of literacy.

questions.stem_md: Many observers in 1951 doubted that India could hold a free election. What was the main reason for their doubt?

options.text_md: India had no written constitution at that time
Only property owners had been given the right to vote
Universal adult franchise was being tried in a very large, mostly poor and largely non-literate society
The Election Commission had not yet been created

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Universal adult franchise was being tried in a very large, mostly poor and largely non-literate society. The doubt came from giving every adult the vote at once in a huge, poor society where most people could not read. The Constitution was already in force (January 1950), there was no property qualification, and the Election Commission existed from 1950.

questions.stem_md: In the 1957 elections, which party formed the government in Kerala, ending Congress rule there?

options.text_md: Communist Party of India
Swatantra Party
Bharatiya Jana Sangh
Socialist Party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Communist Party of India. The Communist Party of India won the 1957 Kerala assembly election and formed a government with E. M. S. Namboodiripad as Chief Minister. The Swatantra Party was founded only in 1959; the Jana Sangh and the Socialists did not win Kerala.

questions.stem_md: Under the first-past-the-post system used in Lok Sabha elections, who wins a constituency?

options.text_md: Only a candidate who gets more than half of all votes cast
The party that wins the most votes in the whole state
Every candidate in proportion to the votes received
The candidate who gets more votes than any other candidate, even if it is less than half

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The candidate who gets more votes than any other candidate, even if it is less than half. First-past-the-post rewards the candidate with the most votes (a plurality), not necessarily a majority. A 50 per cent rule would need run-offs; seats are won constituency by constituency, not state-wide; proportional sharing is a different system.

questions.stem_md: In the first three general elections, the Congress won around three-quarters of Lok Sabha seats while winning less than half of the votes. Which explanation is correct?

options.text_md: The Election Commission gave extra seats to the largest party
The opposition vote was divided among many parties, so Congress came first in most constituencies under first-past-the-post
Votes for opposition parties were not counted in many states
Congress candidates were elected unopposed in most constituencies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The opposition vote was divided among many parties, so Congress came first in most constituencies under first-past-the-post. With the non-Congress vote split among several parties, Congress often won with a plurality, and first-past-the-post turns pluralities into seats. No bonus seats exist; votes were counted normally; unopposed wins were rare.

questions.stem_md: How did the method of voting change after the early elections described in this chapter?

options.text_md: Separate boxes per candidate gave way to a single ballot paper with names and symbols, and later to electronic voting machines
Voting by show of hands replaced secret ballots
Voters began to vote only for parties, not for candidates
Voting was made possible only through the post

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Separate boxes per candidate gave way to a single ballot paper with names and symbols, and later to electronic voting machines. In the first two elections each candidate had a box; later a single ballot paper carrying all names and symbols was marked; electronic voting machines came in from the late 1990s and were used across the country by 2004. The other changes never happened.

questions.stem_md: The third general election, in which the Congress again won a large majority in the Lok Sabha, was held in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1962. The general elections of this era were held in 1951–52, 1957 and 1962. The fourth general election, which changed the picture, came in 1967.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Party symbols were essential in the first general elections in India.

**Reason (R):** A large share of voters at that time could not read the names of candidates.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: symbols let non-literate voters identify their candidate.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Congress won far more seats in the first Lok Sabha than its share of votes alone would suggest.

**Reason (R):** The Election Commission was set up as an independent body in 1950.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. The seat bonus came from first-past-the-post and a divided opposition, not from the creation of the Election Commission.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the first general election only men above 21 years of age could vote.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** From the first election every citizen aged 21 or above, woman or man, could vote: universal adult franchise. (The voting age was lowered to 18 later, in 1989.)

questions.stem_md: True or false? The first general election was widely judged a success because it was held peacefully and its results were accepted, even by those who lost.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Despite the doubts, the first election was held peacefully and fairly enough that losers accepted the results; observers abroad also noted this.

questions.stem_md: The first Chief Election Commissioner of India was ___.
questions.solution_md: Sukumar Sen led the Election Commission during the first general election.

questions.stem_md: The electoral system in which the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority, is called the ___ system.
questions.solution_md: This is the first-past-the-post (plurality) system used for the Lok Sabha.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of early Indian democracy in the order in which they happened.

options.text_md: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh is founded
The Swatantra Party is founded
A Communist Party government takes office in Kerala
The Election Commission of India is set up
The first general election ends and the first Lok Sabha meets

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (a) → (e) → (c) → (b). Election Commission (January 1950) → Jana Sangh (1951) → first Lok Sabha (1952) → Kerala government (1957) → Swatantra Party (1959).

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: In the imagined state of Sonpradesh, 500 thousand valid votes were cast in five constituencies, and Party P received 186 thousand of them. What was Party P's share of the votes (in per cent)?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Vote share = votes of P ÷ total votes × 100.
Step 2: 186 ÷ 500 × 100 = 37.2. So 37.2%.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined state of Sonpradesh, Party P won 37.2% of the votes and 4 of the 5 seats. By how many percentage points did P's seat share exceed its vote share?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Seat share = 4 ÷ 5 × 100 = 80%.
Step 2: Gap = 80 − 37.2 = 42.8 percentage points.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined constituency of Amarpur, P got 40 thousand votes, Q 35 thousand and R 25 thousand. P won the seat. What percentage of voters in Amarpur voted for candidates other than the winner?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Votes against the winner = 35 + 25 = 60 thousand out of 100 thousand.
Step 2: 60 ÷ 100 × 100 = 60. So 60%: the winner was elected though most voters chose someone else.

questions.stem_md: Mention two practical difficulties the Election Commission faced in organising the first general election.
questions.solution_md: Any two real difficulties: size of the electorate, rolls and constituencies, staff, non-literate voters, distances.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Drawing up the electoral rolls** and delimiting constituencies for a **huge electorate** of about 17 crore adults, many entered for the first time.
2. **Training lakhs of staff** and arranging booths and boxes when **most voters could not read**, so symbols were needed.

questions.stem_md: How can a party win most seats in a legislature without winning most votes? Explain with reference to the Congress in the early elections.
questions.solution_md: Link the rule (plurality wins) with the divided opposition.

answer.model_answer_md: Under **first-past-the-post**, a candidate needs only **more votes than any rival**. In the early elections the **opposition vote was split** among many parties, so Congress candidates **came first in most constituencies** with pluralities and won about three-quarters of seats on **less than half** of the votes.

marking_scheme.step: Divided opposition and the result for Congress

questions.stem_md: Why is the 1957 election in Kerala remembered as a landmark?
questions.solution_md: Who won and why it was unusual; what it showed about dominance (and its dismissal).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Communist Party of India** won the assembly election and formed a government under **E. M. S. Namboodiripad**, one of the first communist governments anywhere to come to power **through a ballot**.
2. It showed that Congress dominance had **limits at the state level**; the government was **dismissed in 1959** under Article 356.

marking_scheme.step: Significance for Congress dominance or its dismissal

questions.stem_md: Some observers in 1951 called India's first general election "a gamble". Explain why it was considered a gamble and why it is regarded as a success.
questions.solution_md: One point on the doubts, one on how they were met, one on the outcome.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Gamble:** it was the largest election held anywhere at that time, with **universal adult franchise** in a poor society where **most voters could not read**, so many doubted it could be fair.
2. **Organisation:** the Election Commission prepared rolls, trained staff and used **symbols and separate boxes** so that everyone could vote secretly.
3. **Success:** polling was **peaceful**, turnout was reasonable, and the **losers accepted the results**, proving that democracy could work in a poor country.

questions.stem_md: Compare the results of the first three general elections (1952, 1957 and 1962) in terms of the position of the Congress.
questions.solution_md: Continuity of dominance, the votes–seats gap, and the Kerala exception.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In **all three**, the Congress won around **three-quarters of Lok Sabha seats** and formed the government at the Centre under Jawaharlal Nehru.
2. Its **vote share stayed below half**, so its seat share was magnified by first-past-the-post and a **divided opposition**.
3. At the state level it ruled almost everywhere, but **Kerala in 1957** elected a communist government, an early sign that dominance was not total.

marking_scheme.step: Vote share below half and why seats were higher

questions.stem_md: Describe how India conducted its first general election in 1951–52 and explain why it is considered an important step for democracy in the world.
questions.solution_md: Body, scale, method, outcome, significance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Body in charge:** the **Election Commission**, set up in 1950 under **Sukumar Sen**, organised the poll.
2. **Scale:** about **17 crore** adults were registered; constituencies were delimited and rolls prepared for the first time on a universal basis.
3. **Method:** since most voters could not read, each candidate had a **symbol** and a separate **ballot box**; polling ran over several months.
4. **Outcome:** the election was **peaceful** and the losers accepted the result; the Congress won a large majority.
5. **Significance:** it showed that **universal adult franchise** could work in a **poor, largely non-literate** country, which many had doubted.

marking_scheme.step: Peaceful conduct and acceptance of results

questions.stem_md: "The dominance of the Congress in the first three elections was partly a product of the electoral system." Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer.
questions.solution_md: Accept the claim in part: explain the effect of the system, then other causes, then a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Partly yes:** under **first-past-the-post**, a plurality is enough, so the Congress, the only party present everywhere, won most constituencies.
2. With the **opposition divided** among socialists, communists, the Jana Sangh and others, the anti-Congress vote did not add up to seats.
3. Hence the Congress won about **three-quarters of seats with less than half of the votes**.
4. **But not only the system:** the Congress also had the **legacy of the national movement**, a **nationwide organisation** and popular leaders.
5. **Conclusion:** the system **magnified** a real lead in popular support; it did not create it.

questions.stem_md: Which was the most important reason for the Congress's strong position in the first decades after independence?

options.text_md: It was the only party allowed by the Constitution
Opposition parties were banned until 1967
It inherited the legacy and organisation of the national movement
It was supported only by industrialists

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It inherited the legacy and organisation of the national movement. The Congress had led the freedom struggle and had an organisation reaching most of the country. The Constitution allowed many parties, opposition parties were legal throughout, and its support came from many social groups, not one.

questions.stem_md: The Congress of the 1950s is often described as a "social and ideological coalition". What does this mean?

options.text_md: It was a formal alliance of several separate parties with a common symbol
It shared power with the opposition in every state government
It allowed only one ideology among its members
It brought together people of different classes, castes, regions and ideas, from left to right, within one party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It brought together people of different classes, castes, regions and ideas, from left to right, within one party. The Congress was one party but held within it farmers and industrialists, urban and rural groups, and socialists as well as conservatives. It was not a formal alliance of parties, did not share power with the opposition, and was not ideologically uniform.

questions.stem_md: How did the Congress of this era deal with factions (groups within the party)?

options.text_md: It expelled every faction that disagreed with the leadership
It required factions to register as separate parties
It did not have any factions at all
It tolerated them and let them compete, which helped it hold together different interests

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It tolerated them and let them compete, which helped it hold together different interests. Factions based on ideas or personal loyalties were tolerated and balanced inside the party, so dissatisfied groups had less reason to leave. Expelling or banning factions was not its practice, and factions certainly existed.

questions.stem_md: How was Congress dominance in India different from one-party rule in countries where other parties are banned?

options.text_md: It was based on a constitutional rule that only one party may govern
It came from the army supporting one party
It rested on winning free and competitive elections in which other parties took part
It existed because elections were not held for many years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It rested on winning free and competitive elections in which other parties took part. The Congress stayed in power by winning regular, competitive elections; opposition parties were free to contest and criticise. There was no constitutional bar, no army role, and elections were held on time.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined state in 1955, a group of Congress members who favour faster land reform form a faction and criticise their own state government. Under the "Congress system", what was the most likely result?

options.text_md: The faction is immediately expelled and forms a new party
The leadership adjusts its policy somewhat, and the faction stays inside the party
The state government is dismissed by the President
The faction is banned from contesting elections

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The leadership adjusts its policy somewhat, and the faction stays inside the party. Inside the Congress system, factions pressed the leadership from within and were accommodated through compromise, so they usually stayed. Expulsion, dismissal of the government or bans were not the normal response.

questions.stem_md: Why is it said that, during this era, much of the real "opposition" operated inside the Congress itself?

options.text_md: Groups within the Congress that disagreed with the leadership checked its decisions, while outside parties were weak in seats
Opposition leaders were all members of the Congress Working Committee
The Constitution required the ruling party to appoint the Leader of the Opposition
There were no other parties at all in Parliament

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Groups within the Congress that disagreed with the leadership checked its decisions, while outside parties were weak in seats. Because opposition parties held few seats, much debate and pressure came from factions inside the Congress. Opposition leaders were not on its committees, the Constitution has no such rule, and other parties did sit in Parliament.

questions.stem_md: Who was the Prime Minister of India throughout the period of the first three general elections?

options.text_md: Lal Bahadur Shastri
Jawaharlal Nehru
Indira Gandhi
Vallabhbhai Patel

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Jawaharlal Nehru. Jawaharlal Nehru was Prime Minister from 1947 until his death in 1964. Shastri followed him in 1964, Indira Gandhi in 1966; Patel was Deputy Prime Minister and died in 1950.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Congress could win the support of very different social groups in the 1950s.

**Reason (R):** It accommodated many interests and ideologies, from the left to the right, within one organisation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: being an inclusive coalition is why so many groups could see the party as their own.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** India was a one-party state between 1952 and 1967.

**Reason (R):** One party won the largest number of seats in all three general elections of this period.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: India had many legal parties and competitive elections; one party was dominant, but it was not a one-party state. R is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the 1950s the Congress was a formal alliance of separate registered parties fighting elections on one symbol.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** It was a single party, though an inclusive one; the "coalition" was of social groups and ideas within it, not of registered parties.

questions.stem_md: Match each feature of the Congress in the 1950s with what it describes.

options.text_md: Legacy of the national movement
Social coalition
Ideological coalition
Tolerance of factions

match_right.text_md: Groups inside the party could compete and press the leadership
Many voters saw it as the party that won freedom
Socialists and conservatives both inside one party
Support from different castes, classes, religions and regions

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each feature matched with its meaning: history (legacy), who supported it (social), what ideas it held (ideological), and how disagreements were managed (factions).

questions.stem_md: Explain the idea that the Congress was a "social coalition" in the years after independence.
questions.solution_md: Who supported it, and why that made it a coalition.

answer.model_answer_md: The Congress drew support from **almost every section of society**: peasants and industrialists, urban and rural people, **different castes, religions and regions**. It began as a party of educated elites but grew into a **broad platform** where many groups felt represented.

marking_scheme.step: Why this made it a coalition

questions.stem_md: How did the tolerance of factions help the Congress remain dominant?
questions.solution_md: Factions reduced the need to exit and made the party responsive.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Groups that were **unhappy with the leadership** could fight their battles **inside the party** instead of leaving to form rivals.
2. Factions acted as a **check and balance**, pulling the party towards the centre and keeping it in touch with many groups.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a "dominant party" democracy and a "one-party" system, using India in the 1950s as an example.
questions.solution_md: Define both and place India in the first category.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **dominant-party democracy**, one party keeps winning **free, competitive elections** while other parties exist and criticise it, as with the Congress in the 1950s. In a **one-party system**, other parties are **not allowed**, so the ruling party faces no real electoral contest.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons for the dominance of the Congress in the first decades after independence.
questions.solution_md: Any three distinct reasons, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Legacy:** it had led the **national movement**, and its leaders were widely known and trusted.
2. **Organisation:** it already had a **network of units** across the country when the first elections came.
3. **Inclusive character:** as a **social and ideological coalition** that tolerated factions, it could keep many groups on board, while the opposition was **divided**.

questions.stem_md: The Congress of the 1950s has been compared to a "platform" rather than a party with one fixed ideology. Explain this with three points.
questions.solution_md: Range of views; groups within it; the middle-ground result.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It held **socialists and conservatives**, **moderates and radicals**, so different ideas were argued out inside it.
2. Groups with their own views, such as the **Congress Socialist Party** before 1948, could work within it.
3. Its policies were usually a **compromise of the middle ground**, which let it appeal to many voters while factions kept the debate alive.

marking_scheme.step: Example of a group working within it

questions.stem_md: Explain the main features of the "Congress system" during the era of one-party dominance.
questions.solution_md: Five features: elections, social base, ideas, factions, the role of the opposition.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Dominance through elections:** the Congress kept winning **free, competitive** elections; it was not a one-party state.
2. **Social coalition:** it drew support from **many classes, castes, religions and regions**.
3. **Ideological coalition:** it accommodated **left, right and centre**, settling on middle-ground policies.
4. **Tolerance of factions:** groups inside it competed openly and acted as an **internal check**.
5. **Weak but active opposition:** opposition parties held few seats, but they **criticised** policies and kept alternatives alive, while much real contest happened **within** the Congress.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the effects of one-party dominance on Indian democracy in its early years.
questions.solution_md: Benefits, risks, the checks that existed, and a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Stability:** a party with a clear majority gave the new state a **stable government** while it faced partition, integration of states and planning.
2. **Consensus-building:** because the Congress held many groups, compromises were reached **inside it**, reducing conflict in society.
3. **Risks:** a weak opposition meant **less scrutiny** from outside, and the line between party and government could blur.
4. **Balance:** factions and an articulate opposition still **checked** the government, and elections stayed competitive.
5. **Judgement:** on balance dominance helped democracy take root, but it also **delayed** the growth of strong alternatives, which emerged after 1967.

questions.stem_md: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was founded in 1951 with whom as its founder-president?

options.text_md: C. Rajagopalachari
Ram Manohar Lohia
A. K. Gopalan
Syama Prasad Mukherjee

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Syama Prasad Mukherjee. Syama Prasad Mukherjee founded the Jana Sangh in 1951. Rajagopalachari founded the Swatantra Party, Lohia was a socialist leader and A. K. Gopalan a communist leader.

questions.stem_md: The Swatantra Party was formed in 1959 mainly in reaction to which development?

options.text_md: The Congress's Nagpur resolution supporting land ceilings, state trading in food grains and cooperative farming
The dismissal of the Kerala government
The war with China
The reorganisation of states on linguistic lines

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Congress's Nagpur resolution supporting land ceilings, state trading in food grains and cooperative farming. Leaders who opposed more state control of agriculture and the economy, after the Congress's 1959 Nagpur resolution, formed the Swatantra Party. The other events had different effects; the war with China came in 1962.

questions.stem_md: An imagined candidate in 1962 promises to remove licences and controls on business, to oppose ceilings on landholdings and to seek closer ties with Western countries. Which party is he most likely to represent?

options.text_md: Communist Party of India
Socialist Party
Swatantra Party
Bharatiya Jana Sangh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Swatantra Party. Free enterprise, fewer controls, opposition to land ceilings and a pro-Western outlook were the positions of the Swatantra Party. The CPI and the Socialists favoured more state action for equality; the main emphasis of the Jana Sangh was national and cultural unity.

questions.stem_md: An imagined election pamphlet of 1953 calls for "one country, one culture, one nation" and for Hindi to be promoted as the official language. Which party most likely issued it?

options.text_md: Swatantra Party
Communist Party of India
Bharatiya Jana Sangh
Socialist Party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Bharatiya Jana Sangh. These were positions of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh. Swatantra stressed free enterprise; the CPI and the Socialists stressed economic equality and the rights of workers and peasants.

questions.stem_md: The socialists who formed the Socialist Party in 1948 had earlier worked as which group?

options.text_md: The Congress Socialist Party, a group inside the Congress formed in 1934
A breakaway group of the Communist Party of India
The Hindu Mahasabha
The Muslim League

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Congress Socialist Party, a group inside the Congress formed in 1934. The Congress Socialist Party was formed within the Congress in 1934; its members left to form the Socialist Party in 1948 when groups within the Congress could no longer have their own organisations. It was not a communist, Mahasabha or League group.

questions.stem_md: After the first general election, which party formed the largest opposition group in the first Lok Sabha, though with only a small number of seats?

options.text_md: Swatantra Party
Bharatiya Jana Sangh
Socialist Party
Communist Party of India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Communist Party of India. The Communist Party of India was the largest opposition group in the first Lok Sabha. Swatantra did not yet exist; the Jana Sangh and the Socialists won fewer seats.

questions.stem_md: Under which provision was the communist government of Kerala dismissed in 1959?

options.text_md: Article 370
Article 356 (President's Rule)
Article 21
Article 32

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Article 356 (President's Rule). The Centre dismissed the Kerala government in 1959 by imposing President's Rule under Article 356. Article 370 dealt with Jammu and Kashmir, Article 21 protects life and liberty, and Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies.

questions.stem_md: An imagined opposition MP of 1955 regularly questions the government's food policy in Parliament and suggests changes. Which role of the opposition does this show?

options.text_md: Keeping the ruling party in check by principled criticism
Running the government in place of the ruling party
Choosing the members of the Election Commission
Approving the budget without debate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Keeping the ruling party in check by principled criticism. Questioning and criticising policy keeps the government accountable, a key role of the opposition even when it is small. The opposition does not run the government, choose the Election Commission, or pass budgets without debate.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the relation between the ruling party and opposition leaders in the early years of independence?

options.text_md: Opposition leaders were not allowed to speak in Parliament
There was considerable mutual respect, and some opposition figures had served in the first, broad-based cabinet
The ruling party and the opposition never cooperated on anything
Opposition parties were merged into the ruling party by law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** There was considerable mutual respect, and some opposition figures had served in the first, broad-based cabinet. Leaders of different parties often respected one another, and the first cabinet included non-Congress figures such as B. R. Ambedkar and Syama Prasad Mukherjee. Opposition MPs spoke freely, cooperation did occur, and no law merged parties.

questions.stem_md: The Communist Party of India split in 1964. The new party formed was

options.text_md: the Praja Socialist Party
the Swatantra Party
the Communist Party of India (Marxist)
the Bharatiya Jana Sangh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the Communist Party of India (Marxist). In 1964 the CPI split and the Communist Party of India (Marxist) was formed. The Praja Socialist Party came from the socialist stream; Swatantra and the Jana Sangh had separate origins.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The opposition parties of the 1950s mattered for Indian democracy even though they won few seats.

**Reason (R):** They kept alternative ideas alive and criticised the government, preventing dissatisfaction from turning against democracy itself.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which the opposition parties of the 1950s contributed to Indian democracy.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions: criticism, accountability, alternatives, training leaders, giving voice to the dissatisfied.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They **criticised the policies** of the Congress government and kept it **accountable**.
2. They **kept alternative ideas alive** and prepared leaders, so that democracy did not depend on one party alone.

questions.stem_md: Mention any two positions of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh in the 1950s.
questions.solution_md: Any two positions stated neutrally.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It stressed **"one country, one culture, one nation"** and promoted **Hindi** as the official language.
2. It called for a **strong, militarily capable India** and **closer integration** of all regions into the Union.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Swatantra Party oppose the Congress's economic policies? Give two points.
questions.solution_md: Free enterprise; opposition to specific agricultural controls.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It believed the state should **not control** the economy so much and favoured **free private enterprise**.
2. It opposed **land ceilings, cooperative farming and state trading** in food grains, which the Congress backed after its Nagpur session in 1959.

questions.stem_md: What does the experience of the Kerala government of 1957–59 tell us about Indian democracy in that era?
questions.solution_md: Limits of dominance; communists accepting elections; the debate on Article 356.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Voters could and did **elect a non-Congress government** in a state, so dominance was **not complete**.
2. A communist party came to power **through elections** and governed within the Constitution.
3. Its **dismissal in 1959** under Article 356, after a protest movement, began a long debate on how the **Centre's power over states** should be used.

questions.stem_md: Why were the opposition parties weak in electoral terms in the 1950s even though their leaders were respected?
questions.solution_md: Division, weak organisation, and the inclusive Congress.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The opposition was **divided** among socialists, communists, the Jana Sangh and others, so the **anti-Congress vote split**.
2. Most of them were **new** and had **small organisations** compared with the Congress network.
3. The Congress, as an **inclusive coalition**, already absorbed many of their ideas and supporters, leaving them little space.

questions.stem_md: Describe the ideas and early history of any four opposition parties of the era of one-party dominance.
questions.solution_md: Four parties with origin and ideas, plus their common role.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Socialist Party:** grew from the **Congress Socialist Party** (1934) and became separate in **1948**; stood for **democratic socialism**; later split into several socialist parties.
2. **Communist Party of India:** worked for change through **Marxism-Leninism**; the **largest opposition group** in the first Lok Sabha; formed the **Kerala government in 1957**; split in **1964**.
3. **Bharatiya Jana Sangh:** founded in **1951** by **Syama Prasad Mukherjee**; stressed **national and cultural unity** and Hindi.
4. **Swatantra Party:** formed in **1959** by **C. Rajagopalachari** and others; favoured **free enterprise** and opposed land ceilings.
5. Together they **criticised** the government and offered **alternatives**, though they won few seats.

questions.stem_md: Compare the Bharatiya Jana Sangh and the Swatantra Party of the 1950s and 1960s on their origins, ideas and support.
questions.solution_md: Origins, main concern, economic stance, support base, common ground.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Origins:** the Jana Sangh was founded in **1951** by **Syama Prasad Mukherjee**; Swatantra in **1959** by **C. Rajagopalachari** and others after the Nagpur resolution.
2. **Main concern:** the Jana Sangh emphasised **national and cultural unity**; Swatantra emphasised **economic freedom**.
3. **Economy:** Swatantra wanted **less state control** and free enterprise; the Jana Sangh focused more on cultural and national questions.
4. **Support:** the Jana Sangh drew support mainly in parts of the **north**; Swatantra attracted **landowners, industrialists and some princely families**.
5. **Common ground:** both **opposed the Congress** and won few seats, but added new voices to democratic debate.
